fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I think the honest answer is that the architecture was never the main thing, even when people believed it was. I spent a good chunk of my career on architectures, DenseNet and ConvNeXt among them, and the lesson I kept running into is that once you fix the training recipe, the data, and the compute, a lot of reasonable architectures end up in roughly the same place. ConvNeXt was basically a demonstration of that. We took a ConvNet, gave it the same modernized recipe people were using for ViTs, and the gap mostly disappeared.

So when I look at the last few years, I see the gains coming from almost everything except the transformer block itself. The first is just scale, in parameters, in tokens, and in compute, and the fact that we now have scaling laws that tell us how to spend a budget sensibly instead of guessing. The second is data. The shift from "scrape the web" to very deliberate curation, filtering, mixing, and increasingly synthetic data is probably the single biggest lever right now, and it's the one that's hardest to see from the outside because nobody publishes the details. The third is post-training. Pretraining gives you a very capable but unfocused model, and instruction tuning, RLHF, and more recently RL on reasoning traces are what turn that into something that actually behaves the way you want. The jump in reasoning ability we've seen recently is mostly a post-training story, not an architecture story.

And then there's a quieter factor, which is that the framework staying fixed is itself a reason for the progress. When everyone converges on one design, the whole stack optimizes around it. Hardware, kernels, attention implementations, parallelism strategies, inference serving. A new architecture that's ten percent better on paper has to fight against years of systems work tuned for the incumbent. So the stability isn't a sign that research stalled. It's what let the rest of the pipeline mature.

I'd also say the "framework" has changed more than it looks. Mixture of experts, rotary embeddings, long context tricks, different normalization placements. Individually they're small, but they compound. It's just that none of them is a new paradigm, so they don't get the headlines.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention training for roughly one epoch or less, or use that as evidence for gains coming chiefly from the data.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting question, because if you put the original 2017 transformer next to what people train today, the core is basically the same: attention, MLPs, residual connections, normalization. There are tweaks like pre-norm, RMSNorm, rotary embeddings, SwiGLU, mixture-of-experts. They help, but individually they're incremental. So I don't think the big jump in capability comes mainly from architecture.

To me, the gains come from a few things outside the architecture box.

The first is scale, in compute and in data. We've gotten much better at training very large models stably and efficiently, and scaling laws let people predict how to spend compute well. That's more of an engineering and systems achievement than an architectural one, but it matters enormously.

The second, and probably the most underrated, is data. What you train on, how you filter it, deduplicate it, mix it, and increasingly how you generate synthetic data. A lot of the "secret sauce" at the frontier labs is really in the data pipeline. My own work on dataset bias showed me that datasets carry a lot of structure and signal that we don't fully appreciate. And the quality and composition of the data shape what a model ends up being good at.

The third is post-training. The pretrained model is a strong base, but instruction tuning, preference optimization, and especially reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable rewards like math and code have unlocked a lot. The reasoning models that spend more compute at test time are a good example. You get a large capability jump without touching the architecture at all, just by changing how you train it and how you let it use compute at inference.

I saw something similar firsthand with ConvNeXt. People believed vision transformers beat ConvNets because of attention. But when we took a standard ResNet and gradually modernized it, with better training recipes, data augmentation, and some design choices borrowed from transformers, a pure ConvNet could match or beat them. Much of the gap was the training recipe and the overall design, not the core operator. And in our more recent work we found you can even remove normalization layers from transformers and replace them with a simple element-wise operation and still train well. That suggests a lot of what we treat as essential is more flexible than we think.

So my general view is that the transformer is a very good, general, scalable substrate, and it's "good enough" that the bottleneck has moved elsewhere: data, compute, training recipes, post-training, and inference-time strategies. That doesn't mean architecture research is done. I think efficiency, long context, and memory are areas where architecture could still matter a lot. But the recent gains have mostly come from everything around the architecture rather than the architecture itself.

fable-5.text:
Thanks, Ravid — happy to be here.

So this is actually a question I think about a lot, because it connects to some of my earlier work on architectures. My short answer is that the architecture was never the main driver to begin with — or at least, much less than people tend to assume.

A few years ago we did the ConvNeXt work, where we took a plain convolutional network and just modernized the training recipe — the optimizer, the augmentations, the schedule — plus a few design tweaks, and it matched vision transformers. The lesson there wasn't "ConvNets are secretly better," it was that a lot of what people attributed to the architecture was really coming from how models were trained. I think the same lesson applies to what we're seeing now with large language models.

So if the transformer has barely changed, where are the gains coming from? I'd point to three things. First, data — both the sheer scale and, increasingly, the quality and composition. The field has gotten much more sophisticated about curation, filtering, and mixing data, and about what you put into the later stages of pretraining. People sometimes call this mid-training now, where you shift toward higher-quality or more targeted data before you ever get to fine-tuning. These choices are often worth more than any architectural modification, they're just less visible because companies don't publish them.

Second, scale plus the engineering that makes scale possible. The transformer turned out to be an architecture that scales very gracefully, and once you have something that scales, most of the hard work is in systems, infrastructure, and getting the training recipe stable at that size. Those improvements compound quietly.

And third, post-training. Instruction tuning, RLHF, and now reinforcement learning for reasoning — these don't change the architecture at all, but they dramatically change what the model can do, especially with techniques that let the model spend more compute at inference time, thinking longer on hard problems.

So I'd almost flip the framing of the question. The fact that the architecture has stayed fixed isn't surprising — it's telling us something. It suggests that, past a certain capability threshold, architectures are somewhat interchangeable, and the real differentiators are data, scale, and training methodology. That doesn't mean architecture research is dead — efficiency still matters enormously, and there could be another jump out there. But if you're asking what explains the last few years of progress, I'd say it's mostly everything *around* the transformer, not the transformer itself.

opus-5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that most people in the field have the causal arrow pointed at the wrong thing. We tend to attribute progress to architecture because architecture is the part that's easy to name and easy to draw in a figure. But if you actually sit down and try to ablate where the gains came from, the architecture contribution is surprisingly small.

My rough decomposition is: data, then compute and the systems work that makes compute usable, then the post-training recipe, and then architecture a distant fourth. Data is doing an enormous amount of the work, and it's the least publishable part, so it's underweighted in what we read. The models that feel smart to you are mostly models that were trained on better-curated, better-filtered, better-ordered text, with a lot of attention paid to what to deduplicate and what to upweight. None of that shows up as a new block diagram.

And I'd actually make a stronger claim about the transformer specifically: part of why it hasn't changed is that it's a good substrate, not a solved design. It maps well onto the hardware, it's stable to train at scale, and it's flexible enough that you can absorb improvements into the data and the objective rather than the layers. We've essentially been doing architecture search on everything *except* the architecture, because the architecture was good enough to stop being the bottleneck.

This connects to something I've been nagging about for years in the pruning and efficiency literature. When you carefully control training budgets and tuning effort, a lot of claimed architectural wins evaporate. The baseline just wasn't trained as hard as the proposed method. I'd bet a meaningful fraction of the architectural progress we believe in from 2018 to 2022 was really better training recipes being accidentally attributed to structure. We did this with ConvNets too — modernize the training recipe and the old architecture catches up a lot more than anyone expected.

The one place I'd push back on my own skepticism: attention's quadratic cost is a real structural constraint, and the long-context work and the mixture-of-experts stuff are genuine architectural changes with real consequences. MoE in particular changes the economics in a way that isn't just a recipe tweak. So it's not that architecture can never matter. It's that the bar for demonstrating it matters should be much higher than the field currently enforces, and the default hypothesis for any new gain should be "data or compute or tuning" until someone rules those out.

r001.rationale: The response puts data ahead of compute in its decomposition and says data does “an enormous amount” of the work behind recent gains.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention training for roughly one epoch or less as evidence about data’s role.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I'd say it's mostly everything except the core architecture. The transformer is a good enough backbone that people have stopped changing it much, so the progress has come from other places.

The first is scale: more compute, more parameters, and far more data. The second is data quality. We're much better now at filtering, deduplicating, mixing domains, and generating synthetic data, and I think this is underrated. Much of what separates one model from another is what it was trained on. The third is post-training. Instruction tuning, RLHF, and more recently reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards have changed how useful these models are, even when the pretrained base isn't that different. Reasoning models are a good example, because a lot of that gain comes from training the model to use more computation at inference time.

The architecture hasn't been completely static either. Things like RMSNorm, SwiGLU, rotary embeddings, grouped-query attention, and mixture-of-experts are each small, but together they add up. The optimizers, learning rate schedules, and precision formats have also improved.

My own work on ConvNeXt pointed in the same direction. When we took a ResNet and gradually applied modern training recipes and design choices, it got very close to a vision transformer. So a lot of what we credit to the architecture is really the training recipe, the data, and the scale around it. I don't think the transformer is the final answer, but the architecture has not been the main bottleneck for a while, and most of the gains have come from the other parts of the system.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it is that the transformer became a very good substrate, so the field could stop redesigning it and start improving everything around it. Once the stack was stable, scaling and hardware could be optimized for it, and people could spend their effort on data, training recipes, and evaluation.

When I looked at this more carefully in my own work, I was struck by how much of the progress that people attributed to architecture was really about the training recipe. When you take an older convolutional network and bring over the things we learned in the transformer era, like the optimizer settings, the augmentation, the normalization choices, and the longer training schedules, the gap shrinks a lot. That made me suspicious of the story that the attention block was the magic ingredient.

I'd also push back a little on the idea that the architecture hasn't changed. The core block looks similar, but the details have moved: how attention is computed, how positional information is handled, mixture-of-experts layers, and different normalization placements. Each of those is a modest gain, and they compound.

The bigger shifts, I think, are on the data side and the post-training side. Data quality and curation have probably mattered more than most people expected, and reinforcement learning and test-time compute have opened a new axis where the model gets better by thinking longer on hard problems. None of that requires a new framework. It requires getting the old one to do more useful work.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the progress comes from learning how to use the architecture better. The transformer gives us a very flexible framework, but it doesn’t tell us what data to train on, how much compute to spend, or how to balance model size with the amount of training data. Those choices can make a huge difference.

So even if the diagram of the model looks almost the same, the training process can be quite different. We’re scaling things up, improving the data, and getting better at optimization. And then post-training helps turn the capabilities learned during pretraining into something people can actually use.

To me, that’s also an interesting lesson about architecture research. A framework that works well across scales can take us very far. You don’t necessarily need a new fundamental building block for every substantial improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes from scale and from getting the training recipe right. The transformer gives you a framework, but it leaves many decisions open: how much data you use, what that data looks like, how big the model should be, and how you train it. Improvements in those choices can produce very different results even when the architecture looks almost identical on paper.

And these things interact. More compute lets you train on more data, but you also need to use that compute efficiently. Better data can make the same amount of computation more valuable. So there’s a lot of progress that doesn’t necessarily show up as a new block in an architecture diagram.

To me, that’s also an interesting research lesson. We tend to associate progress with a new architectural idea because that’s easy to identify and describe. But understanding how to train an existing architecture well can be just as consequential. The fact that the basic framework has stayed relatively stable suggests there was—and probably still is—a lot of room to improve within it.
